name: Normcore

lead: Normcore is a style of dressing in deliberately ordinary clothes: plain T-shirts, hoodies, chinos, jeans and generic sneakers. People adopt it to look put-together without looking like they are trying, and to blend into many social settings.

The word came from the trend-forecasting group K-HOLE in its 2013 report Youth Mode, where it described finding freedom in being nothing special. A February 2014 New York magazine article by Fiona Duncan turned it into a fashion label, and the term was a runner-up for Oxford University Press's 2014 neologism of the year.

paras: Wardrobes are built from basics from mass retailers such as Uniqlo or the Gap, in neutral colours and relaxed fits, with sneakers instead of dress shoes. There is no fixed formula, and the look is worn day to day.
There are no health risks. The commentary around it is mainly about its meaning, with writers noting that the word was often read differently from how its coiners intended.

Normcore: Fashion Movement or Massive In-Joke?

chain: Approachable look that fits many settings
angle.text: People wear normcore as a simple way to look neat and unfussy without chasing trends. The staple pieces are cheap and widely available.

lead: Normcore is a fashion style and cultural attitude centred on plain, average-looking clothing. In appearance terms it offers a clean, approachable and low-effort presentation made from basics such as T-shirts, hoodies, polo shirts, chinos, jeans and sneakers. [1]

The term first appeared in 2008 in a webcomic by Ryan Estrada and was used in 2013 by the trend forecasting group K-HOLE in Youth Mode: A Report on Freedom, where it meant finding liberation in being nothing special. [1] Grokipedia credits K-HOLE members including Emily Segal and describes it as code-switching so a person can fit in anywhere. [2]

On 26 February 2014 Fiona Duncan's article in New York magazine linked normcore to dressing neutrally to avoid standing out, which popularised the fashion meaning. [1] Hacker News threads from 2014 show readers debating whether it was a movement or an in-joke. [3][3]

paras: Typical normcore pieces include hoodies, T-shirts, polo shirts, sweatpants, chinos, jeans, shorts and sneakers, while suit jackets, ties and dress shoes are generally avoided. Retailers associated with the style include the Gap, Uniqlo and Jack & Jones. [1]

K-HOLE's 2013 report described the term as an attitude. The 2014 New York article merged it with a separate K-HOLE idea of dressing neutrally, which Wikipedia describes as a misreading that became the popular usage. [1] The Gap ran ads directed by David Fincher in August 2014, and The Guardian covered its rise that December. [1]

Oxford University Press named normcore runner-up for neologism of the year in 2014, and the AP Stylebook added the word in 2016. [1] A women's variant called menocore, describing loose neutral clothing, was discussed in 2017. [1]

K-HOLE member Emily Segal said it was about contextualisation and belonging rather than privileging individuality. [2] Writers interpreted the style as a reaction to constantly changing trends because its clothes are seen as timeless. [1]
